rationale:
Today's slate stays inside GLP-1 and follows the 10-18 playbook. Retatrutide is our strongest Shorts lane (median 98 views), drug-first question titles work, both drugs get named in comparisons, and only next-gen decoders do well as long-form.

L1 is a retatrutide vs tirzepatide decoder in our breakout format ("Did [new drug] beat tirzepatide?"). It isn't a repeat of the 09-30 TRIUMPH-2 results video because it leads with the triple-hormone mechanism and how to read comparisons across trials. The body rests on peer-reviewed evidence: the Phase 2 trial (NEJM 2023), TRIUMPH-2 (Lancet), SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022) and the label for the GLP-1 and GIP mechanism. TRIUMPH-3 gets one line, credited to Lilly. That keeps it verifiable in depth rather than resting on breaking news.

S1 spins off L1 with the dated "Is retatrutide approved yet? (Oct 2026)" question, our best Instagram format and best YouTube lane. The bootleg death reports are only a hook credited to CBS. The full death-report angle ran on 10-14, so I didn't repeat it.

S2 is early on the new ANESTHESIOLOGY surgery-outcomes study (emerging, low competition). It builds on the anesthesia Short that got 83 views and is a positive benefits-beyond-weight angle with careful observational hedging.

S3 is the contrarian-but-true correction in the head-to-head lane, which is rising. Semaglutide 7.2 mg (Wegovy HD) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) have never been compared in a randomized trial. The only head-to-head, SURMOUNT-5, used semaglutide 2.4 mg.

C1 is an evergreen framework for keeping results long term, refreshed with the BMJ meta-analysis on regain. Carousels still reach almost nobody, but the quota asks for one, so it's a save-worthy list with no stopping advice.

Pillars: research ×2, beyond-weight, myths, life-on-glp1. Body systems vary (metabolism and weight, regulation, heart and surgery, comparison, maintenance). Everything I skipped was either flagged caution with thin new evidence (alcohol, eyes, cost, PCOS), weak for us (orforglipron Shorts), or covered within the last 30 days (muscle, response spread, SURMOUNT-5 side effects, bootleg deaths).

pieces.topic: Retatrutide, the triple-hormone agonist (GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors): how it works and how its trial results compare with tirzepatide's, with a dated status
pieces.angle: Keep the decoder exactly as planned, with these locks: hook 'Did retatrutide beat tirzepatide? No trial has compared them. In a 48-week Phase 2 trial, the top dose averaged 24.2%.' TRIUMPH-2 uses the Lancet figures only (12.7% / 19.1% / 20.8% vs 4.0% placebo at 80 weeks, 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight), with the estimand named and A1C taken from the paper. TRIUMPH-3 is 'Lilly reported up to 22.6% at 80 weeks in adults with severe obesity and established cardiovascular disease'. Status: 'Not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of Oct 2026. Lilly says it plans to submit to the FDA in Q1 2027.' Keep the FDA warning about online products, the per-arm side effects, the 'don't switch or stop' line and the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Did Retatrutide Beat Tirzepatide? How the Triple-Hormone Shot Works (24.2%, Phase 2)
pieces.why: Decoders of next-gen drugs are our only long-form lane that travels (median ~32, EloraTZP 396). Lilly's Q3 earnings around Oct 29 and the bootleg news are driving demand, and the body rests on peer-reviewed NEJM and Lancet papers. | fact-check: Topic and structure are sound and fit the strongest long-form lane (next-gen decoder, 'Did X beat tirzepatide?'). Checked: Phase 2 top dose 24.2% at 48 weeks (NEJM 2023). TRIUMPH-2: 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight, 4/9/12 mg for 80 weeks. Weight loss was 12.7%, 19.1% and 20.8% vs 4.0% on placebo, published in The Lancet and presented at EASD 2026 (epocrates). Lilly's 23 Jul 2026 topline gave the same 20.8% vs 3.2% placebo and an A1C fall of up to 1.6%, against about 1.4–1.5% in the paper. The two figures most likely use different estimands, so they will conflict unless labelled. TRIUMPH-3 per Lilly: up to 22.6% at 80 weeks in adults with severe obesity and established cardiovascular disease. Lilly plans a BLA submission to the FDA in Q1 2027 (Lilly press release, HCPLive 23 Jul 2026). Problems to fix: (a) use only the Lancet placebo figure (4.0%) and its A1C figure, name the estimand, and don't mix in the topline 3.2% or 1.6%; (b) the hook number 24.2% comes from a 48-week Phase 2 trial in people without diabetes, so the first line has to say 'Phase 2, 48 weeks' and answer 'no head-to-head' right away; (c) TRIUMPH-3 population is 'severe obesity with established cardiovascular disease', credited as 'Lilly reported'; (d) write the filing plan as 'Lilly says it plans to submit to the FDA in Q1 2027'. That's a plan, not a filing or an approval.

pieces.topic: Is retatrutide approved yet? A dated status check for the US, UK, Canada and Australia (Oct 2026)
pieces.angle: First line: 'Is retatrutide approved yet? Not yet. As of Oct 2026 it isn't approved by the FDA, the UK's MHRA, Health Canada or Australia's TGA.' Then: 'Lilly reported Phase 3 results in July 2026 and says it plans to submit to the FDA in early 2027. A plan to file isn't approval.' One number: 'In TRIUMPH-2, published in The Lancet, adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight lost 20.8% on the top dose vs 4.0% on placebo over 80 weeks.' Then: 'CBS News reported the FDA received at least two death reports after people used products sold as retatrutide. Reports don't show the product caused the deaths, but the FDA warns these products aren't the trial drug.' One GI line, the prescriber or clinical-trial route, 'follow for more' and the prescriber line.
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. Retatrutide is our strongest Shorts lane (182/98/63), the dated status question is our best Instagram format (patch, 85 reach), and death-report coverage is pushing status searches up. Slot it at 08:00 or 13:00. | fact-check: Matches our best Instagram format (a dated status question) and the retatrutide lane. Checked: Lilly announced TRIUMPH-2/-3 results in Jul 2026 and plans an FDA submission in Q1 2027. CBS News reported FDA documents showing at least two death reports this year tied to illicit products sold as retatrutide, not linked to Lilly's trials (Gizmodo, Newsweek and others citing CBS). Fixes: (a) the placebo figure conflicts between sources: the Lancet paper says 4.0%, Lilly's topline says 3.2%. Use the Lancet figure, credit it to the paper and keep the estimand consistent with L1; (b) say 'at least two' death reports, credited to CBS News reporting on FDA documents, and keep 'a report doesn't show the product caused the death'; (c) write 'Lilly says it plans to submit', not 'will file'. The death-report line must stay calm, not fear-bait: put it after the status answer, not as the opener. No vials, sellers, doses or sourcing.

pieces.topic: Surgery outcomes on GLP-1 medicines: 2.03 million elective-surgery records linked GLP-1 use to lower odds of major heart complications and infections (ANESTHESIOLOGY, Oct 2026, observational)
pieces.angle: Title: 'GLP-1 Medicines (Like Mounjaro) and Surgery: Fewer Heart Complications?' First line: 'In about 2 million surgery records, people taking GLP-1 medicines had 11% lower odds of major heart complications after elective surgery. That's a link, not proof.' Give the population (adults, elective surgery over 1 hour, at least 24 hours in hospital, 2016–2024, 145,610 on a GLP-1) and the 8% lower odds of infection. Credit 'presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 meeting', plus the researchers' line that it doesn't prove cause and effect. Practical line: 'Tell your surgeon and anesthesia team you take a GLP-1, because these medicines can slow stomach emptying, and follow their plan.' One GI line and the prescriber line. On screen: 'observational · conference data · elective surgery >1 hr · odds, not proof'.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) or Semaglutide Before Surgery: Fewer Heart Complications?
pieces.why: Published Oct 18 with low competition, so we're early. It builds on our anesthesia Short (83 views), puts a named drug first in a question title, and is a positive benefits-beyond-weight angle. | fact-check: The study exists, but its venue is misdescribed. It was presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 annual meeting (the ASA conference) in Oct 2026, not published in the journal Anesthesiology, so it's a conference abstract that hasn't been peer-reviewed in full (Newswise / ASA press release, MedicalXpress Oct 2026). Confirmed: 2,028,601 adults had elective surgery lasting more than 1 hour with at least 24 hours in hospital, Jan 2016–Dec 2024, and 145,610 were on GLP-1 therapy. Results: 11% lower odds of major cardiovascular complications (heart attack, heart injury, stroke or death) and 8% lower odds of postoperative infection. The authors say it doesn't prove cause and effect. Fixes: (a) on-screen and spoken attribution becomes 'presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 meeting, not yet a full published paper'; (b) the press materials may not give absolute rates per group. If the abstract doesn't, don't invent them: say 'absolute rates weren't reported in the summary'; (c) the working title implies tirzepatide and semaglutide were tested specifically, but the study covers GLP-1 therapy in general. Lead with 'GLP-1 medicines' and use brands only as recognisable examples, if the source names them; (d) in 2016–2024 most users were probably on older GLP-1s, so don't claim drug-specific results; (e) don't confirm the 'matched' claim unless the source says it. Keep 'tell your surgeon and anesthesia team', with no holding or timing advice.

pieces.topic: Semaglutide 7.2 mg (Wegovy HD) vs tirzepatide (Zepbound): has there been a head-to-head trial? The SURMOUNT-5 dose gap explained
pieces.angle: Answer by 10 s: 'No. Semaglutide 7.2 mg hasn't been tested against tirzepatide in a randomized trial. The only head-to-head, SURMOUNT-5, used semaglutide at up to 2.4 mg.' SURMOUNT-5 (adults with obesity without diabetes, 72 weeks, maximum tolerated doses): tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg 20.2% vs semaglutide 1.7 or 2.4 mg 13.7%. STEP UP (adults with obesity without diabetes, 72 weeks): semaglutide 7.2 mg 18.7% vs semaglutide 2.4 mg 15.6% (treatment-policy). Novo reported 20.7% for 7.2 mg (trial-product). Label it 'Separate trials, not head-to-head.' FDA approved 7.2 mg in Mar 2026 for adults who've tolerated 2.4 mg and need more weight loss. Optional neutral lawsuit line: 'Novo Nordisk is suing Lilly over these ad comparisons; Lilly disputes it; no ruling yet.' One GI line, 'don't switch or stop on your own', and the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide 7.2 mg (Wegovy HD) vs Tirzepatide (Zepbound): Ever Tested Head to Head? #shorts
pieces.why: Our proven named head-to-head lane (SURMOUNT-5 at 157 and growing) gets a fresh, rising hook from the lawsuit headlines. It's a myth-correcting piece that names both drugs and both doses. | fact-check: A useful, accurate correction that fits the head-to-head lane. Checked: the FDA approved Wegovy HD (semaglutide 7.2 mg) in Mar 2026 (HCPLive 19 Mar 2026) for adults with obesity or overweight who have tolerated 2.4 mg for at least 4 weeks and need more weight loss. STEP UP: 1,407 adults with obesity without diabetes, 72 weeks. Weight loss was 18.7% on 7.2 mg vs 15.6% on 2.4 mg (treatment-policy), and Novo reported 20.7% for the trial-product estimand. Novo sued Lilly in Jul 2026 (D.N.J., Lanham Act), alleging that ads compared Zepbound's top doses with lower Wegovy doses. Lilly says it stands behind the SURMOUNT-5-based ads and there's no verdict yet (Reuters via CTV and others). Fixes: (a) SURMOUNT-5's semaglutide arm was the maximum tolerated dose of 1.7 or 2.4 mg, and tirzepatide was 10 or 15 mg. Saying only '2.4 mg' overstates it, so use 'semaglutide 1.7 or 2.4 mg (maximum tolerated)'; (b) STEP UP compared 7.2 mg with 2.4 mg and placebo, not with tirzepatide; (c) present both STEP UP estimands with labels, treatment-policy 18.7% first; (d) give the approval population as 'adults who have tolerated 2.4 mg and need more weight loss'; (e) source the lawsuit to a confirmed primary news report. The Pharmaphorum article wasn't located, so use Reuters/CTV or verify Pharmaphorum before citing it, and include Lilly's response. Keep it under 170 words: drop the lawsuit if it pushes the script over.

pieces.topic: Keeping results on a GLP-1 long term: obesity as a chronic condition, what SURMOUNT-4 and the BMJ regain meta-analysis show, and evidence-based habits that support results
pieces.angle: Slide 4: 'A BMJ review of 37 studies (9,300+ people) found weight came back at about 0.4 kg a month on average after weight-management medicines were stopped. For newer drugs like semaglutide and tirzepatide it was about 0.8 kg a month, and the authors projected a return to starting weight in about 1.5 years. Regain was about 0.3 kg a month faster than after diet-and-exercise programmes ended. These are averages and modelled projections, not a prediction for any one person.' SURMOUNT-4 slide: per-arm weight change after the switch to placebo vs continued tirzepatide, with group sizes and weeks. Keep the habit slides marked 'recommended, not proven on the drug', with the kidney caveat on protein and 'start gently' on exercise. Last slide: disclaimer, 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own', and the full prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Keeping GLP-1 Results Long Term: What the Evidence Says Helps
pieces.why: The regain question is rising (BMJ meta-analysis, ScienceAlert Oct 18), and a habits framework is the kind of list people save. It's evergreen and well sourced, with an encouraging chronic-care tone. | fact-check: The framework is safe and evidence-based, but slide 4 misstates the BMJ meta-analysis (Weight regain after cessation of medication for weight management: systematic review and meta-analysis, BMJ, Jan 2026, PubMed 41500720). It covered 37 studies and more than 9,300 people. Average regain across all weight-management drugs was about 0.4 kg a month. About 0.8 kg a month applies to newer drugs (semaglutide and tirzepatide), with a projected return to baseline weight in about 1.5 years. Regain after stopping drugs was about 0.3 kg a month faster than after behavioural programmes ended (Oxford/NIHR BRC release, Science Media Centre). The '0.1 kg a month after behavioural programmes' figure wasn't confirmed, so verify it in the paper or replace it with the confirmed 'about 0.3 kg a month faster' comparison. Label the projections as modelled and the comparison as indirect (across studies). Also: carousels have reached 0–3 accounts on all 20 posts. The topic is good, but the owner should consider rebuilding it as a Short such as 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): what happens to weight after stopping?' (SURMOUNT-4).
